title: Moving together
objectives: Compute covariance and correlation from a joint table.

screens.title: Two assets, one table
screens.prose: Each cell is one day's pair of returns for assets A and B, with its probability. The nine chances add to 1.
screens.question: How do A and B tend to move?

options.text: Together: when one rises, the other usually rises
Opposite: when one rises, the other usually falls
options.why: You read the small corners, 0.02 each. The big chances, 0.20 each, sit where both rise or both fall.

options.text: No pattern: each has its own spread
options.why: You looked at each asset alone. The joint table shows the pairs, and the same-direction corners carry 0.40 between them.

hints.text: Find the largest chances in the corners.
Both down and both up each have chance 0.20.
Up with down has only 0.02, in each direction.

feedback.correct: Same-direction days are ten times as likely as opposite days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the corner where both rise with the corner where A rises and B falls.

explain.text: Both up and both down each have chance 0.20. A up with B down has 0.02, and so does the reverse. So the two assets mostly move together.

screens.title: Same side, other side
screens.prose: Both means are 0%, so a positive return is above the mean. For each cell, multiply A's return by B's. The product is positive when both sit on the same side.
screens.question: Shade every cell where the product of the two returns is positive.

hints.text: $(-1)(-1) = +1$. Which other cell gives a positive product?
A zero return makes the product 0, not positive.

feedback.correct: Both down and both up give $+1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade only the cells where both returns are non-zero with the same sign.

byKey.flat: You included the cell where both are flat. Its product is $0 \times 0 = 0$: it pushes neither way.
byKey.opp: You shaded the opposite corners. There $(-1)(+1) = -1$, a negative product.
byKey.r1c2: B is flat there, so the product is 0.
byKey.r2c1: A is flat there, so the product is 0.

explain.text: Two cells give $+1$: both down and both up, with 0.20 each. Two give $-1$, with 0.02 each, and the rest give 0. The positive cells carry far more chance.

screens.title: Covariance
screens.prose: Weight each product of distances from the means by its chance, and add. That is the **covariance**: $$\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = E[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)].$$ Here both means are 0, so it is $E[XY]$.
screens.question: What is $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)$, in units of $\%^2$?

hints.text: Only four cells have a non-zero product.
The positive cells give $1 \times 0.20$ each; the negative ones $-1 \times 0.02$ each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add product times chance over all nine cells.

byKey.same: You counted only the same-direction cells. The opposite corners subtract $2 \times 0.02$.
byKey.added: You added the opposite corners. Their product is $-1$, so they subtract.
byKey.count: You added the products without their chances. Weight each by its probability.

explain.text: The same-direction cells add $0.40$ and the opposite cells take away $0.04$. So $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 0.36$, in $\%^2$. Positive covariance means the two tend to sit on the same side of their means.

screens.title: Means that are not zero
screens.prose: New assets, with returns −1% or +2% for A and −1% or +3% for B. Now subtract the means. A shortcut, which we prove later: $$\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y].$$
screens.question: Complete the table.

hints.text: For $E[XY]$, the four products are $1$, $-3$, $-2$ and $6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work down the table; each line uses the ones above.

byKey.r2c1: Multiply each cell's two returns, weight by its chance: $1(0.3) - 3(0.2) - 2(0.1) + 6(0.4)$.
byKey.r3c1: Subtract the product of the means, $0.5 \times 1.4 = 0.7$, from $E[XY]$.

explain.text: $E[X] = 0.5$, $E[Y] = 1.4$ and $E[XY] = 1.9$. So $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 1.9 - 0.7 = 1.2$. Without subtracting $0.7$, the means alone would look like co-movement.

screens.title: Correlation
screens.prose: Covariance carries units, $\%^2$ here. Divide by both standard deviations, $\sigma_X = 1.5$ and $\sigma_Y = 1.96$, to get the **correlation** $$\rho = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}.$$ It has no units.
screens.question: What is $\rho$ for these two assets?

hints.text: Multiply the two sds first.
$1.5 \times 1.96 \approx 2.94$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the covariance by the product of the two sds.

byKey.cov: That is the covariance. Divide it by $\sigma_X\sigma_Y$.
byKey.vars: You divided by the variances, 2.25 and 3.84. Use the sds, 1.5 and 1.96.
byKey.onesd: You divided by $\sigma_X$ only. Divide by $\sigma_Y$ too.

explain.text: $\rho = 1.2/2.94 \approx 0.41$: a moderate tendency to move together. Correlation always lies between $-1$ and $1$. The extremes mean the points lie exactly on a straight line.

screens.title: Seeing correlation
screens.prose: Each dot is one simulated day: A's return across, B's up, both in standard deviation units. Move $\rho$ from 0.8 to 0, then to $-0.8$.
screens.question: At $\rho = -0.8$, where does B tend to be on days when A is well above its mean?

options.why: You read the sign the wrong way round. Negative correlation tilts the cloud down: high A comes with low B.
Each day is random, but the cloud has a tilt. At $-0.8$ the right side of the cloud sits low.

hints.text: Set $\rho$ to $-0.8$ and look at the dots on the right.
Dots far to the right are days when A is well above its mean.

feedback.correct: Negative correlation: when A is high, B tends to be low.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\rho = -0.8$ and look at the right-hand dots.

explain.text: At $\rho = 0.8$ the cloud tilts up, at 0 it is round, and at $-0.8$ it tilts down. The sign says which way; the size says how tightly the dots hug a line.

screens.title: Steeper is not stronger
screens.prose: Fund C holds three times asset B, so its return is $3Y$. The left cloud is A against B, with $\rho = 0.8$. The right is A against C.
screens.question: What is the correlation between A and C?

options.text: $0.8$, the same as A with B

options.why: You read correlation as the slope of the line. The slope triples to 2.4, but $\rho$ can never exceed 1.

options.text: Between 0.8 and 1, since the cloud is steeper
options.why: You judged strength by steepness. The dots hug their line exactly as tightly as before; only the scale changed.

options.text: Three times as strong, since the covariance triples
options.why: Covariance does triple, but it carries units. Correlation divides by $\sigma_C = 3\sigma_Y$, which takes the 3 back out.

hints.text: How do the two fitted slopes compare?
Every C value is B's value times 3; the scatter around the line is stretched by 3 as well.
$\rho(X, 3Y) = \dfrac{3\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X \cdot 3\sigma_Y}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\rho(X, 3Y)$ with the definition and cancel.

byKey.slope: You read correlation as a slope. The slope tripled to 2.4, but $\rho$ lies between $-1$ and $1$.
byKey.cov: You compared covariances across different units. Correlation removes the units, and it stays 0.8.

explain.text: The covariance triples and so does $\sigma_C$, so $\rho$ stays 0.8. The slope, $\mathrm{Cov}/\mathrm{Var}(X)$, triples from 0.8 to 2.4. Correlation measures how tight the line is, not how steep.

screens.title: Zero, yet linked
screens.prose: $X$ is $-1$, 0 or 1, each with chance 1/3, and $Y = X^2$. Once you know $X$, you know $Y$ exactly.
screens.question: Which is true?

options.text: $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$, yet $X$ and $Y$ are not independent

options.why: You read zero covariance as no link. Here $Y$ is fixed by $X$; covariance only catches a straight-line tilt.

options.text: $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) > 0$, since $Y$ grows as $X$ moves away from 0
options.why: You looked at the right half only. On the left, $Y$ rises as $X$ falls, and the halves cancel.

hints.text: Compute $E[XY] = E[X^3]$ and $E[X]$.
$X^3$ is $-1$, 0 or 1 with equal chances.
$E[XY] = 0$ and $E[X] = 0$, so the covariance is $0 - 0 \times E[Y] = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the covariance, then ask whether knowing $X$ tells you $Y$.

byKey.indep: You treated zero covariance as independence. Knowing $X = 1$ forces $Y = 1$, so they are dependent.

explain.text: $E[XY] = \tfrac{1}{3}(-1 + 0 + 1) = 0$ and $E[X] = 0$, so the covariance is 0. Yet $Y$ is a function of $X$. Independence gives zero covariance, but not the other way round; level 4 tests independence properly.

screens.title: The shortcut, proved
screens.prose: Prove the shortcut you used. The means $\mu_X$ and $\mu_Y$ are fixed numbers.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $= E[XY - \mu_Y X - \mu_X Y + \mu_X\mu_Y]$, multiply out the brackets

hints.text: Start from the definition.
Multiply out before using linearity.
Definition, expand, linearity, substitute the means, collect.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Change one thing per line, starting from the definition.

byKey.lin: Linearity acts on a sum, so multiply out the brackets first.
byKey.sub: Substitute the means after linearity has produced $E[X]$ and $E[Y]$.

explain.text: With $Y = X$ this is $E[X^2] - \mu^2$, the variance shortcut: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathrm{Cov}(X, X)$. Correlation then rescales: $\rho = \mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$, between $-1$ and $1$.

screens.title: Two stocks
screens.prose: Two stocks' daily returns, simplified to three outcomes each. A moves ±1%, B moves ±3%. Both means are 0%.
screens.question: What is the correlation $\rho$ between A and B?

hints.text: Find $\sigma_X$ and $\sigma_Y$ from the row and column totals.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the covariance and both sds, then divide.

byKey.cov: That is the covariance, in $\%^2$. Divide by $\sigma_X\sigma_Y = 1.5$.
byKey.vars: You divided by the product of variances, 2.25. Use the sds, whose product is 1.5.
byKey.nosub: You used only the same-direction corners, $0.9/1.5$. The opposite corners subtract $0.12$.

explain.text: $\mathrm{Cov} = 0.90 - 0.12 = 0.78$, $\sigma_X = 0.707$ and $\sigma_Y = 2.121$. So $\rho = 0.78/1.5 = 0.52$. Many pairs of large stocks have daily correlations near this.

screens.title: A hedge ratio
screens.prose: You hold £100,000 of stock B and want to hedge with stock A, from the same table. The hedge ratio is $$\beta = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\mathrm{Var}(X)}:$$ short £$\beta$ of A for each £1 of B.
screens.question: How much of A should you short, in £?

hints.text: B moves about three times as much as A, but not in lockstep.
$\beta = 1.56$; multiply by £100,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the covariance by A's variance, then scale by £100,000.

byKey.rho: You used $\rho$ as the ratio. It has no units; $\beta$ also accounts for B moving more than A.
byKey.vol: You used the ratio of sds, 3. That would be right only if $\rho = 1$; $\beta = \rho \sigma_Y/\sigma_X = 1.56$.
byKey.wrongvar: You divided by B's variance. The hedge instrument is A, so divide by $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

explain.text: $\beta = 0.78/0.5 = 1.56$, so short £156,000 of A. The hedge cuts B's variance from 4.5 to $4.5 - 0.78^2/0.5 = 3.28$. With $\rho = 0.52$, much of B's risk is its own and cannot be hedged with A.

ideas: Covariance averages the product of distances from the means: positive when the two sit on the same side.
Correlation $\rho = \mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$ removes the units and lies between $-1$ and $1$.
Independent variables have zero covariance, but zero covariance does not prove independence.
summary.trap: Correlation is not a slope, and covariances in different units cannot be compared. Scaling either variable leaves $\rho$ unchanged.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by the product of the sds.

byKey.vars: You divided by the variances, 4 and 25. Use the sds.
byKey.cov: That is the covariance. Correlation divides by $\sigma_X\sigma_Y$.
byKey.sum: You divided by the sum of the sds. Use their product.

explain.text: $\rho = 6/10 = 0.6$, a fairly strong tendency to move together.

quiz.question: What is the correlation of $X$ with the fund's return?

options.why: You doubled $\rho$ with the position. The sd doubles too, and cancels the 2.
You doubled and added the shift. Shifts change neither covariance nor sd, and the 2 cancels.

options.text: It cannot be found without the sds
options.why: You expected units to matter. They cancel: $\rho(X, 2Y) = \rho(X, Y)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out $\mathrm{Cov}(X, 2Y)$ and $\sigma_{2Y}$.

explain.text: $\mathrm{Cov}(X, 2Y + 0.01) = 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)$ and $\sigma_{2Y} = 2\sigma_Y$. The 2s cancel, so $\rho$ stays 0.3.

quiz.prose: On days when an airline's shares rise above their mean, oil tends to be below its mean, and the reverse.
quiz.question: What is the sign of their covariance?

options.why: You read any link as positive. Opposite sides of the means give negative products.
Zero would mean no straight-line tilt. Here one tends to be high when the other is low.

feedback.correct: Opposite sides of the means give negative products.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is the sign of $(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)$ on a typical day?

explain.text: On a typical day one distance is positive and the other negative. Their product is negative, so the covariance is negative.
